short-description: Minecraft minigame network with its own server architecture, seven games, and a community site.
description: A Minecraft server network running up to 500 slots, built on a family of in-house plugins named after berries, with seven minigames, a progression system, and a Symfony site plugged into a XenForo forum.
long-description:
BerryGames was a Minecraft minigame network, and the oldest thing in this portfolio: the first commit lands in September 2018, on a minigame plugin called WitchRush.

The architecture was split across a family of plugins, each named after a berry. GooseBerry was the BungeeCord proxy routing players between servers, CloudBerry the Spigot API shared by every game, SkyBerry the server core, and StrawBerry a REST API exposing player data to the website. A Hub held the lobby, with its own progression showing coins, credits, level, and experience.

Seven minigames ran on top: SkyWars, BedWars with eight teams and diamond generators, GroundFall and its TNT scoring, Catfight, Pvpwall, Pitchout, and WitchRush. Players earned blueberries and credits, and end-of-game screens summarised what each round had given them.

Staff had tools inside the game rather than a separate back office: a friends system, and a server management menu switching a server between Public, Beta VIP, and Maintenance without leaving Minecraft.

The public face was a Symfony site plugged into a XenForo forum, listing live player counts per game next to the Discord feed. A React redesign was started in early 2021 and never finished. The nine repositories were archived between 2020 and 2022.

challenges.multi-server-architecture: Routing players across several servers while keeping the network feeling like one place
challenges.shared-player-state: Carrying currencies, levels, and progress between games running on separate servers
challenges.game-loop-per-minigame: Writing a distinct game loop, scoreboard, and reward table for each of the seven games
challenges.moderation-at-scale: Giving staff the tools to run the network from inside Minecraft rather than a back office
challenges.forum-integration: Plugging a Symfony site into a XenForo forum so accounts and posts stayed in one place

learnings.infrastructure-before-content: Most of the work went into the proxy, the API, and the core before a single game could ship
learnings.community-is-the-product: Player counts and the Discord mattered more to the network than any individual feature
learnings.git-hides-the-team: Builders, moderators, and community staff left no commits, so the repositories credit a fraction of the people involved
learnings.minecraft-as-a-school: Running a network taught server architecture, moderation, and release management earlier than any client project would have

future-plans.archived-repositories: All nine repositories are archived, and the network is offline
